n: Manasseh becomes king at only twelve and reigns fifty-five years—the longest reign of any king of Judah. Its length makes his influence on the nation enormous.

f.g: Her name means “my delight is in her”; compare Isaiah 62:4.

n: Manasseh copies the very practices of the Canaanite nations that God had driven out of the land, undoing the purpose for which Israel was given it.
He reverses his father’s reforms, rebuilding shrines and altars to Baal and Asherah, and worshipping the sun, moon and stars—just like the notorious King Ahab of Israel.

f.g: Hilltop shrines; Hezekiah had removed them to centralize worship at the temple (2 Kings 18:4).
Hebrew Asherah—a wooden pole or image of the Canaanite fertility goddess.
The sun, moon and stars worshipped as gods, a practice tied to Assyrian and Canaanite religion.

n: Shockingly, Manasseh puts pagan altars inside the Lord’s own temple, the place God chose to bear His name.

f.w: In Jerusalem will I put my name

n: He fills both temple courtyards with altars to the stars, turning the house of the Lord into a center of idol worship.

f.g: The inner court for priests and the outer court for the people.

n: Manasseh sacrifices his own son in fire and dabbles in every kind of occult practice the law of Moses forbade. Each act was a deliberate rejection of the Lord.

f.g: Child sacrifice by burning, associated with the god Molech.
Practiced fortune-telling, perhaps reading omens to pick lucky days.

n: He even sets up an Asherah idol in the temple, defying God’s promise to place His name there forever. The contrast between God’s purpose and Manasseh’s act is stark.

f.g: A carved idol.

f.w: will I put my name for ever

n: God had promised Israel lasting security in the land—but always on condition of obedience to His law given through Moses.

f.w: only if they will observe to do

n: The people did not listen. Manasseh led them into even worse evil than the nations God had removed from the land before Israel.

f.g: Led them astray; enticed them.

n: God does not stay silent; He sends prophets to warn the king and people. Jewish tradition holds that Isaiah was martyred under Manasseh, though the Bible does not say so.
The Lord’s charge: Manasseh has outdone even the Amorites, the original inhabitants infamous for their wickedness, and has dragged Judah into sin with him.

f.g: A name for the pre-Israelite peoples of Canaan, whose sins had led to their removal (Genesis 15:16).

n: The coming disaster will be so terrible that anyone who hears of it will be stunned. The prophets saw this fulfilled in Jerusalem’s fall to Babylon.
Using builders’ tools as images, God says He will measure Jerusalem by the same standard He used for Samaria and Ahab’s house—and wipe it clean like a dish turned upside down to dry.

f.g: A measuring line; Jerusalem will be judged by the standard that brought Samaria’s destruction in 722 BC.
A plumb line, used to see whether a wall is straight.

f.w: as a man wipeth a dish
f.g: Completely emptied and cleaned out.

n: Even the surviving remnant of God’s people will be handed over to enemies to be plundered.

f.g: Judah, the last remaining part of Israel after the northern tribes were exiled.

n: God explains that this judgment is the result of a long pattern of rebellion stretching back to the Exodus, not just one king’s sins.

f.w: since the day their fathers came forth out of Egypt

n: Beyond idolatry, Manasseh murdered many innocent people, filling Jerusalem with bloodshed. Violence and false worship went hand in hand.
The usual closing note points to fuller royal records. 2 Chronicles 33 adds that Manasseh was taken captive to Babylon, repented, and was restored—a remarkable story of mercy.
Manasseh is buried in a palace garden rather than in the royal tombs of David, perhaps a sign of his dishonor. His son Amon succeeds him.

f.g: A royal garden, location unknown; perhaps named for a former owner.

n: Amon becomes king at twenty-two but reigns only two years.

f.g: A town probably in Galilee, suggesting a political marriage with northern families.

n: Amon follows his father’s evil path without the repentance Manasseh later showed.
He worships all the idols his father had worshipped, continuing the corruption of the land.

f.g: “Walk” is a Hebrew idiom for how one lives.

n: The summary is blunt: Amon abandoned the God of his ancestors.

f.g: Abandoned, turned away from.

n: Amon’s own officials assassinate him in his palace—one more sign of instability under wicked rule.
The landowning citizens of Judah execute the assassins and crown Amon’s eight-year-old son Josiah, who will become one of Judah’s greatest kings.

f.g: Likely the free landowners of Judah, an influential group that protected David’s royal line.

n: The standard closing formula points readers to the official royal annals for more on Amon.

f.w: book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah
f.g: Official court records now lost, not the biblical books of Chronicles.

n: Amon is buried in the same garden as his father, and Josiah takes the throne. The story is about to turn toward hope.

f.g: Tomb.
